teile.einleitung: Atoms are the tiny building blocks that all substances are made of, from water and air to our own bodies. An atom has a small, heavy nucleus and a shell of electrons. Today 118 different kinds of atom are known: the chemical elements.
wichtigste: The word atom comes from the Greek “átomos” and means indivisible.
The Greek philosopher Democritus already taught that everything is made of atoms.
An atom is about one ten-millionth of a millimetre across.
The nucleus consists of protons and neutrons, the shell of electrons.
An atom consists almost entirely of empty space.
An atom is electrically neutral because it has as many protons as electrons.
Hydrogen has the simplest atom, with just one proton.
Today 118 chemical elements are known (as of 2025).

abschnitte.text: As early as the 5th century BC the Greek philosopher **Democritus** taught that everything is made of tiny, indivisible particles. He called them átomos, which means indivisible. He could not prove it. Only around 1808 did the Englishman **John Dalton** develop a scientific atomic theory that could explain chemical reactions.

In the centre lies the **atomic nucleus**, made of positively charged **protons** and uncharged **neutrons**. Round the nucleus is the shell with the negatively charged electrons. Because an atom has as many protons as electrons, it is electrically neutral from outside. The number of protons decides which element it is. Hydrogen has one proton, carbon six and gold 79.

An atom is about one ten-millionth of a millimetre across. If you enlarged an atom to the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would only be as big as a pea in the middle. Even so, almost all the mass is in the nucleus. The rest is almost entirely **empty space**, in which the tiny electrons move about.

In 1897 Joseph John Thomson discovered the **electron**. In 1911 Ernest Rutherford found out that an atom has a tiny, heavy nucleus. In 1913 the Dane Niels Bohr presented his **Bohr model of the atom**, in which the electrons circle the nucleus on fixed orbits, rather like planets round the sun. Today the electrons are described with quantum physics as clouds in which they are likely to be found. In 1932 James Chadwick discovered the neutron.

Atoms with the same number of protons form a **chemical element**. Today 118 elements are known, arranged in the periodic table. Atoms can join together to form **molecules**, for example two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom to make a water molecule. The whole variety of substances in the world is built up from these compounds.

At **CERN** in Geneva scientists from all over the world study the smallest building blocks of matter. At the Paul Scherrer Institute in Aargau atoms and particles are studied with large facilities. In 1905 in Bern, Albert Einstein wrote a paper that helped prove that atoms exist. With modern scanning tunnelling microscopes, developed at IBM in Rüschlikon, individual atoms can even be made visible.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tiny, heavy centre of the atom, made of protons and neutrons.
A positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.
An uncharged particle in the atomic nucleus.
A tiny, negatively charged particle in the shell of the atom.
A substance that consists only of atoms with the same number of protons.

gewusst: A single drop of water contains more atoms than there are stars in the Milky Way.
The scanning tunnelling microscope, with which you can see atoms, was invented at IBM in Rüschlikon and won the Nobel Prize in 1986.
Most of the hydrogen atoms in our body date from the time shortly after the Big Bang.

teile.einleitung: An atomic clock is the most accurate clock there is. Instead of a pendulum or a quartz crystal, it counts the tiny, extremely regular vibrations of atoms. Good atomic clocks do not go wrong by even one second in many millions of years.
wichtigste: An atomic clock measures time with the help of the vibrations of atoms.
Since 1967 the second has been defined by the caesium-133 atom and no longer by the movement of the Earth.
A second lasts exactly 9,192,631,770 periods of the radiation of caesium-133.
The first working caesium atomic clock ran in Great Britain in 1955.
The long-wave transmitter DCF77 broadcasts the time for radio-controlled clocks in central Europe.
Without atomic clocks, satellite navigation with GPS would not work.
Optical atomic clocks are even more accurate, because they use a much higher frequency of vibration.

abschnitte.text: Every clock needs something that repeats itself very regularly, for example a pendulum. In an atomic clock it is the electrons in the atoms, which can only take in very particular amounts of energy. If microwaves with exactly the right **frequency** are shone on caesium atoms, they react especially strongly. A control loop keeps the microwaves exactly at this frequency, and electronics count the vibrations.

In the past the second was determined by the rotation of the Earth or its path round the sun. The Earth, however, does not turn completely evenly; it is slowed down slightly by the tides, for example. That is why in 1967 it was decided to define the **second** using caesium-133. Since then a second has been exactly 9,192,631,770 vibrations of this radiation.

The first working caesium atomic clock went into operation in 1955 at the National Physical Laboratory in Great Britain. It was built by Louis Essen and Jack Parry. Today there are so-called **caesium fountains**, in which atoms are gently tossed upwards and fall back down. The newest optical atomic clocks work with laser light and atoms such as strontium or ytterbium.

abschnitte.titel: World time and the leap second
abschnitte.text: Many atomic clocks in institutes all over the world are compared with each other and averaged. This produces **International Atomic Time, TAI**. Because the Earth turns irregularly, civil time has been adjusted to the Earth’s rotation now and then since 1972 with a **leap second**. Experts have decided to abolish leap seconds by 2035 at the latest.

Every GPS satellite contains atomic clocks. A navigation device calculates its position from the travel time of the radio signals, which move at the speed of light. If a clock is wrong by just one microsecond, the position is already around 300 metres out. **Radio-controlled clocks** in homes receive the time signal from the DCF77 transmitter near Frankfurt am Main and set themselves in this way.

In Switzerland the Federal Institute of Metrology, **METAS**, in Bern-Wabern is responsible for official time. Several atomic clocks run there and are compared with clocks abroad. In this way Swiss time feeds into worldwide atomic time. Station clocks, computers and mobile phones also ultimately get their exact time from such atomic clocks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A soft metal whose atoms are used to define the second.
Tells you how often something vibrates per second.
An extra second used to adjust the time to the rotation of the Earth.
A clock that sets itself to the correct time using a radio signal.

gewusst: The most accurate optical atomic clocks would not have gone wrong by even one second since the Big Bang.
Atomic clocks are so accurate that they show that time passes a tiny bit faster on a high mountain than in the valley.
A radio signal that travels for one microsecond covers around 300 metres.

teile.einleitung: Atomic physics is the branch of physics that studies the structure of atoms. Above all it investigates the electrons in the shell of the atom and how atoms give out or take in light. Without atomic physics there would be no lasers, no atomic clocks and no LED lamps.
wichtigste: Everything around us is made of tiny atoms.
An atom has a positively charged nucleus and a shell of negatively charged electrons.
Rutherford’s scattering experiment with a gold foil showed that atoms have a tiny, positively charged nucleus.
In diameter an atom is about ten thousand to a hundred thousand times bigger than its nucleus.
Isotopes of an element differ in the number of neutrons in the nucleus.
Electrons can only take on certain energy levels.
Every element gives out light with very particular colours, its spectral lines.

abschnitte.text: Atoms are the smallest building blocks of the chemical elements. An atom is about one ten-millionth of a millimetre across. In the centre sits the **atomic nucleus** of protons and neutrons, and round it move the **electrons**. The number of protons decides which element it is; for example, hydrogen has one and carbon six.

Around 1909, researchers in Ernest Rutherford’s laboratory fired alpha particles at an extremely thin **gold foil**. Most simply flew through, but a few were strongly deflected or even bounced back. In 1911 Rutherford concluded from this that almost all the mass sits in a tiny, positively charged **nucleus**. So the atom is mostly empty space: if the nucleus were the size of a pinhead, the atom would be as big as a football stadium.

abschnitte.titel: The Bohr model of the atom
abschnitte.text: In 1913 the Danish physicist Niels Bohr developed a new model. In it the electrons only circle on certain orbits with fixed energies, the **energy levels**. In the hydrogen atom the electron in its ground state has an energy of minus 13.6 electronvolts. If an electron jumps from a higher to a lower orbit, it gives out a particle of light, a **photon**. In the jump from n = 2 to n = 1 this photon has an energy of 10.2 eV.

If you send the light of a glowing gas through a prism, you see individual coloured lines instead of a rainbow. These **spectral lines** are like a fingerprint of the element. For hydrogen, the series of lines in the visible range is called the **Balmer series**, named after the Basel teacher Johann Jakob Balmer, who found a formula for it in 1885. With spectral lines astronomers can find out what distant stars are made of.

Atoms of the same element always have the same number of protons, but not always the same number of neutrons. Such variants are called **isotopes**. Carbon-12 and carbon-14, for example, are two isotopes of carbon. Carbon-14 is radioactive and is used to work out the age of bones or wood.

Atomic physics is found in many everyday devices. **Lasers** in barcode readers and **LED** lamps work because electrons jump between energy levels. Atomic clocks use the vibrations of atoms and are extremely accurate; they also control satellite navigation. In Switzerland the Federal Institute of Metrology, METAS, runs atomic clocks for official Swiss time.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tiny, heavy centre of an atom, made of protons and neutrons.
A very light, negatively charged particle in the shell of the atom.
A particle of light, that is a small packet of light energy.
A tiny unit of energy used in atomic physics.
A kind of atom of an element with a particular number of neutrons.

gewusst: Johann Jakob Balmer from Basel was actually a maths teacher at a girls’ school when he found his famous formula.
If you removed all the empty space from the atoms of the whole of humanity, the remaining matter would fit into a cube about the size of a sugar cube.

teile.einleitung: The contact area is the surface with which an object rests on what is underneath it. Its size determines how strongly the object presses on the ground. That is why you sink in less with snowshoes than with hiking boots.
wichtigste: The contact area is the surface where a body touches what it rests on.
Pressure is force divided by area.
The bigger the contact area, the smaller the pressure for the same weight.
A small contact area produces a high pressure.
The unit of pressure is the pascal; 1 Pa is 1 newton per square metre.
Many wheels, wide caterpillar tracks and snowshoes spread the weight over a large area.
Knives and nails use a tiny area to produce a high pressure.

abschnitte.text: Every object that stands or lies on something touches the surface underneath with a certain area. This area is called the **contact area**. A brick has three sides of different sizes that you can lay it on. Its weight always stays the same, but the contact area changes. This also changes how strongly it presses on the ground.

**Pressure** is the force divided by the area: p = F : A. Its unit is the **pascal**, named after the Frenchman Blaise Pascal. A brick weighing 30 N on 0.02 m² produces a pressure of 1500 Pa. If you stand it on its smallest side, the pressure is greatest. If you lay it on its largest side, the pressure is smallest.

A **piste basher** has wide caterpillar tracks instead of wheels so that it does not sink into the snow. For the same reason walkers wear snowshoes in winter and skiers wear skis. Heavy lorries have many wheels so that the weight is spread over a larger area. A house stands on a wide **foundation** so that it does not sink into the ground. Good rucksacks also have wide shoulder straps that spread the load and press less.

Narrow stiletto heels can damage a wooden floor, because the small area produces a high pressure. A person weighing 60 kg on a thin heel presses harder on the floor than an elephant on its wide foot. Sometimes, though, high pressure is wanted. The tip of a **nail** or the edge of a knife is tiny. That way they go into wood or bread with little force.

If someone has fallen through thin ice, they should move lying flat. That way the weight is spread over a large area and the ice breaks less easily. Helpers also crawl towards them flat on their stomachs or push a ladder or a board over the ice. It is safest, however, only to walk on frozen lakes when they have been officially declared safe. In Switzerland many municipalities announce when natural ice is safe.

begriffe.erklaerung: The surface with which a body rests on what is underneath it.
Force per area, measured in pascals.
The unit of pressure, one newton per square metre.
The wide, solid base of a building in the ground.

gewusst: Thanks to its wide, soft soles, a camel hardly sinks into the desert sand.
A fakir can lie on a bed of nails because his weight is spread over hundreds of nails.
The mountain hare in the Alps has wide, thickly furred hind paws, with which it sinks less deeply into the snow.

teile.einleitung: Buoyancy is the force with which water or air pushes a body upwards. That is why you feel lighter in the swimming pool, and why even huge ships made of steel float. The principle was discovered by the Greek scientist Archimedes more than 2000 years ago.
wichtigste: Buoyancy is a force that acts upwards in liquids and gases.
It arises because the pressure at the bottom of a body is greater than at the top.
Buoyancy is as great as the weight of the displaced liquid.
The buoyant force is measured in newtons.
For a fully submerged body, buoyancy does not depend on its mass but on its volume.
A ship made of steel floats because it is hollow inside and full of air.
There is also buoyancy in air, which is why hot-air balloons rise.

abschnitte.text: When you get into the bath, **the water rises**, because your body needs space. The water presses on you from all sides, but more strongly from below than from above. This results in an upward force, **buoyancy**. That is why a heavy stone is easier to lift in water than on land, and why air bubbles rise.

The Greek scientist **Archimedes** lived in the 3rd century BC in Syracuse on Sicily. According to legend he recognised the principle in the bath and shouted “Eureka”, which means “I have found it”. **Archimedes’ principle** says: a body experiences a buoyancy as great as the weight of the liquid it displaces. It applies in all liquids and gases.

Buoyancy is calculated from the **density** of the liquid, the submerged volume and the gravitational factor g. A body with a volume of 0.5 dm³ displaces exactly 0.6 kg of water in salt water of 1.2 kg per dm³. With g equal to 10 N/kg, this gives a buoyancy of about **6 newtons**. How heavy the body itself is does not matter for buoyancy, only its volume.

If the buoyancy is greater than the weight, a body floats; if it is smaller, it sinks. A steel ship floats because its **hollow hull** displaces a great deal of water. A **submarine** fills tanks with water to dive and blows them empty with air to rise. Divers wear a lead belt so that they can dive more easily.

Air also produces buoyancy, but much less than water, because it is lighter. A **hot-air balloon** rises because the warm air in the balloon is lighter than the cool air outside. In 1783 the Montgolfier brothers launched the first manned hot-air balloon in France. Every winter a big international balloon festival takes place in Château-d'Oex in Vaud.

abschnitte.titel: Examples from nature and everyday life
abschnitte.text: Many fish have a **swim bladder**, with which they control their buoyancy. In the Dead Sea you can lie on the water almost without moving, because the very salty water has a high density. Life jackets contain foam or air and so increase buoyancy. The passenger boats on Swiss lakes also use Archimedes’ principle.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which a liquid or a gas pushes a body upwards.
The water that a body pushes aside when it goes in.
How much mass there is in a certain volume.
A gas-filled organ with which fish hover in the water.

gewusst: An egg sinks in tap water, but floats in very salty water.
Only about a tenth of a large iceberg sticks out of the water.
People float better after breathing in, because the air in the lungs increases buoyancy.

teile.einleitung: Archimedes of Syracuse was a Greek mathematician, physicist and inventor who lived in the 3rd century BC. Among other things, he discovered why things float or sink in water and explained the law of the lever. He is regarded as one of the greatest scientists of ancient times.
wichtigste: Archimedes lived from about 287 to 212 BC in Syracuse on Sicily.
He explained why things float or sink in water.
According to a story, he had his famous idea in the bath.
Afterwards he is said to have shouted “Eureka”, which means “I have found it”.
King Hiero II had him check whether a crown was made of pure gold.
Archimedes described how heavy things can be lifted with a lever.
The Archimedean screw carries water upwards.

abschnitte.text: Archimedes was born around 287 BC in **Syracuse**, a Greek city on the island of Sicily. He was probably acquainted with King Hiero II and worked for him. Archimedes studied mathematics, physics, astronomy and technology. Many of his writings have survived to this day.

The Roman writer **Vitruvius** passed down a famous story. King Hiero II feared that his goldsmith had mixed silver into the gold of his crown. While bathing, Archimedes noticed that his body pushed water aside, and he shouted out excitedly: **Eureka**. A crown containing silver pushes aside more water than a lump of gold of the same weight, because silver has a lower density and needs more room. Galileo Galilei later suspected that Archimedes was more likely to have tested the crown with a balance under water.

Archimedes recognised that a body in water experiences **buoyancy**. This is exactly as great as the weight of the water that the body pushes aside. If a body displaces 2 litres of water, the buoyancy is about 20 newtons. If the buoyancy is greater than the weight of the body, it floats; otherwise it sinks.

Archimedes described the **law of the lever**: with a long lever you can lift heavy loads with little force. The famous saying that he could move the Earth if he were given a fixed point comes from him. The **Archimedean screw**, a spiral inside a tube, carries water upwards. When Syracuse was being defended, he is said to have built war machines such as giant grabbing arms.

Archimedes calculated the number pi astonishingly accurately by drawing polygons inside and around a circle. He found that pi lies between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7. He also calculated the areas and volumes of spheres and cylinders. He was especially proud of the discovery that a sphere has two thirds of the volume of the cylinder that fits round it.

In 212 BC the Romans captured the city of Syracuse during the Second Punic War. Archimedes was killed by a Roman soldier, even though the general wanted to spare him. According to legend, he said beforehand: “Do not disturb my circles.” His grave is said to have shown a sphere inside a cylinder.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which water pushes a body upwards.
Tells you how heavy a substance is for the same volume.
A bar with which you can move a lot with little force.
Greek for: I have found it.
The water that a body pushes aside when it is put in.

gewusst: A crown of pure gold with a mass of 965 grams has a volume of only 50 cubic centimetres, because gold is very dense.
According to the story, after his discovery Archimedes ran through the streets of Syracuse without any clothes on.
A crater on the Moon is named after Archimedes.

teile.einleitung: Resolving power tells you how well an eye, a microscope or a telescope can still see two points that are close together as separate. If it is too small, the points blur into a single spot. The better the resolving power, the finer the details you can see.
wichtigste: Resolving power gives the smallest distance or angle that can still be seen as separate.
Because of the diffraction of light, every optical instrument has a limit of resolution.
In 1873 Ernst Abbe worked out the resolution limit of the light microscope.
Light with a shorter wavelength allows better resolution.
Telescopes with a larger aperture can tell apart finer details in the sky.
A healthy human eye resolves about one minute of arc.
In 2014 Stefan Hell received the Nobel Prize for STED microscopy, which gets round the Abbe limit.

abschnitte.text: Imagine two little lamps shining side by side in the distance. Close up you see two lights; from far away only one. The smallest distance or **angle** at which you can still see two separate points describes the resolving power. It applies to eyes, cameras, microscopes and telescopes.

Light is a wave, and waves are diffracted at openings. That is why a point of light is never shown as a perfect point, but as a small disc with rings. If two such discs lie too close together, they overlap. According to the **Rayleigh criterion**, for a round opening with diameter D the smallest angle is about 1.22 times the wavelength divided by D.

The bigger the mirror or lens of a telescope, the finer its resolution. The Hubble Space Telescope has a mirror 2.4 metres in diameter. For green light of 550 nanometres, this gives about 0.058 seconds of arc. On Earth, however, the shimmering **turbulence of the air** gets in the way, which is why telescopes are built on high mountains or sent into space.

In 1873 the German physicist **Ernst Abbe** showed that a light microscope can only separate structures down to about half the wavelength of light. More precisely, the limit depends on the wavelength and the **numerical aperture** of the objective lens. With light of 500 nanometres and a numerical aperture of 1.4, it is about 179 nanometres. A drop of immersion oil between the objective and the specimen increases the numerical aperture and so improves the resolution.

With light of shorter wavelength, such as blue or ultraviolet light, you can see finer details. Electron microscopes use electrons, whose wavelength is much smaller than that of light, and so can even make out the arrangement of individual atoms. Stefan Hell developed **STED microscopy**, in which fluorescent dyes are cleverly switched on and off. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this in 2014.

A healthy eye can resolve about one minute of arc, which is a sixtieth of a degree. With this, from about 3.5 metres away you can still make out two points one millimetre apart. In an eye test at the eye doctor’s, it is exactly this **visual acuity** that is measured. With screens, people also talk about resolution, meaning the number of pixels.

begriffe.erklaerung: Waves spread out sideways too behind an opening or an edge.
A sixtieth of a degree, that is a very small angle.
A number that tells you how much light an objective lens can collect.
The distance from one wave crest to the next.

gewusst: An eagle can resolve much more finely than a human and spots a mouse from a great height.
Several radio telescopes round the Earth were linked together and in 2019 produced the first image of a black hole.

teile.einleitung: ATLAS is one of the biggest and most complicated particle detectors in the world. It stands at the CERN research centre near Geneva in a huge cavern deep underground. With ATLAS, researchers detected the long-sought Higgs boson in 2012.
wichtigste: ATLAS is a particle detector at CERN’s LHC particle accelerator.
The name originally stood for “A Toroidal LHC ApparatuS”.
The detector is around 46 metres long and 25 metres high.
ATLAS is bigger, but lighter, than the CMS detector.
Like an onion, ATLAS consists of several layers with different tasks.
A trigger system selects the interesting collisions for storage in real time.
In 2012 ATLAS and CMS together detected the Higgs boson.

abschnitte.text: In the **LHC**, CERN’s Large Hadron Collider, protons race round a ring 27 kilometres long at almost the speed of light. They collide at four points, and that is where the big detectors stand. **ATLAS** is the biggest of them and stands near Meyrin in the canton of Geneva. It is around 46 metres long and 25 metres high and weighs about 7000 tonnes. The CMS detector is smaller but about twice as heavy.

ATLAS consists of several layers round the collision point. Inside, the **inner detector** measures the tracks of charged particles. Because a strong magnetic field bends their paths, their momentum can be worked out from the curvature. Around it lie the **calorimeters**, which slow particles down and so measure their energy. Right on the outside sits the **muon spectrometer**, because muons pass through the inner layers almost unhindered.

The name ATLAS refers to the **toroid magnets**, which are arranged in a ring round the detector. They are superconducting and have to be cooled to very low temperatures for this. Their eight big coils give the detector its typical appearance. The magnetic fields bend the particles so that they can be measured.

In the detector, bunches of protons collide up to 40 million times a second. No computer could store that much data. That is why the **trigger system** selects the interesting collisions in real time and throws the rest away. Particles such as neutrinos, which fly through the detector unnoticed, are recognised by ATLAS through **missing momentum** at right angles to the beam.

On 4 July 2012 the ATLAS and CMS teams announced the discovery of a new particle, the **Higgs boson**. It explains why other elementary particles have mass. A year later Peter Higgs and François Englert, who had predicted the particle, received the Nobel Prize in Physics. Several thousand researchers from many countries work together on ATLAS, including from Swiss universities.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measuring instrument that tracks down and measures particles from collisions.
The Large Hadron Collider, the largest particle accelerator in the world, at CERN.
A part of a detector that measures the energy of particles by slowing them down.
An elementary particle similar to the electron but around 200 times heavier.
An elementary particle connected with how mass comes about.

gewusst: ATLAS is about half the size of Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris.
The ATLAS cavern lies around 100 metres underground.
ATLAS weighs about as much as the Eiffel Tower.

teile.einleitung: Archimedes’ principle explains why ships float and stones sink. It says: a body in a liquid experiences a buoyant force that is as great as the weight of the liquid it displaces. It was discovered by the Greek scholar Archimedes more than 2200 years ago.
wichtigste: The buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced liquid.
It is calculated as the density of the liquid times g times the displaced volume.
Archimedes described the law in his work “On Floating Bodies”.
Archimedes lived in the 3rd century BC in Syracuse on Sicily.
A floating body sinks until buoyancy and weight are equal.
The principle also applies in gases, for example in air.
The principle can be used to find the density of bodies and liquids.

abschnitte.text: **Archimedes** was a Greek mathematician, physicist and inventor. He lived from about 287 to 212 BC in Syracuse on Sicily. He invented, for example, the Archimedean screw for raising water and studied levers. He wrote down his law about buoyancy in the work **“On Floating Bodies”**. According to a well-known legend he shouted “Eureka!”, I have found it, when the idea came to him in the bath.

When a body is put into a liquid, it pushes part of the liquid aside. This **displaced liquid** has a weight. The **buoyant force** that pushes the body upwards is exactly as great. As a formula: buoyancy = density of the liquid · g · displaced volume. A cube with sides of 10 cm, completely submerged, displaces 1 litre of water and experiences about 10 N of buoyancy.

An aluminium cube with a volume of 1 dm³ weighs 27 N. In water it experiences 10 N of buoyancy, so a spring balance only shows 17 N. A ball with a volume of 2 dm³ that is half submerged displaces 1 dm³ and experiences 10 N of buoyancy. A block of wood with a density of 0.6 g/cm³ is 60 per cent submerged when it floats. If a stone with a mass of 600 g displaces 200 ml of water, it has a **density** of 3 g/cm³.

A famous story tells of King Hiero II of Syracuse. He wanted to know whether his new crown was made of pure gold or whether the goldsmith had mixed in silver. Archimedes is said to have measured the volume of the crown with water and compared it with a bar of gold of the same weight. Silver has a lower density than gold and would have displaced more water. Whether the story really happened exactly like this, nobody knows.

The principle explains why a ship made of steel floats: its hull displaces a great deal of water. A **hydrometer** is a small glass tube that floats in a liquid and shows its density on a scale. This is used, for example, to check the sugar content of grape juice in winemaking. Air also produces a small buoyancy. A very precise balance therefore shows a slightly smaller value for a large block of polystyrene in air than in a vacuum.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which a liquid or a gas pushes a body upwards.
The pushing aside of liquid by a body that is put into it.
Mass per volume; it tells you how heavy a substance is for the same size.
A floating instrument for measuring the density of liquids.

gewusst: Archimedes is said to have said: “Give me a fixed point and I will lift the world off its hinges.”
In Switzerland the hydrometer for the sugar content of grape must is also called an “Öchslewaage”.
In water a person can carry a friend much more easily than on land, because buoyancy helps.

teile.einleitung: The asynchronous or induction motor is the most common electric motor in the world. It drives pumps, fans, conveyor belts, lifts and even locomotives. Its trick: a rotating magnetic field drags the rotor round with it, without any current having to flow to it through contacts.
wichtigste: An induction motor usually runs on three-phase current, which produces a rotating field.
The rotor always turns a little more slowly than the rotating field.
The relative difference between the speed of the rotating field and the rotor is called slip.
The most common type of rotor is the squirrel-cage rotor.
Galileo Ferraris and Nikola Tesla developed the principle at about the same time.
If you swap two of the outer conductors, the motor turns the other way.
With a frequency converter the speed can be adjusted continuously.

abschnitte.text: An induction motor consists of two main parts. The fixed part is called the **stator** and contains copper coils. The turning part is called the **rotor**. In the most common type, the **squirrel-cage rotor**, the rotor contains bars of aluminium or copper joined at the ends by rings. It looks like a hamster wheel or a cage.

The three-phase current in the stator coils produces a **rotating field**, a magnetic field that goes round in a circle. This field cuts across the bars of the rotor and induces a current in them. The current forms its own magnetic field, and the rotor is dragged round by the rotating field. If the rotor turned exactly as fast as the field, no more current would be induced. That is why it always lags a little behind; it runs asynchronously.

At 50 hertz the rotating field turns, depending on the design, at 3000 or 1500 revolutions per minute, for example. The difference from the rotor is called **slip**. If the field turns at 1500 and the rotor at 1440 per minute, the slip is 60 : 1500 = 4 per cent. If the motor is loaded more heavily, the slip rises a little. With a **frequency converter** you change the frequency of the current and can thus adjust the speed continuously.

When an induction motor is switched on directly, a very high starting current flows briefly. It is around five to eight times the rated current. Larger motors are therefore often started with a **star-delta starter**, which lowers this current. If you want to reverse the direction of rotation, you simply swap two of the three outer conductors.

The Italian **Galileo Ferraris** and the inventor Nikola Tesla developed the principle of the rotating-field motor at about the same time in the 1880s. Around 1889 Mikhail Dolivo-Dobrovolsky built the first practical squirrel-cage motor at AEG in Berlin. In 1891 three-phase current was transmitted over a long distance for the first time, from Lauffen am Neckar to Frankfurt. The Oerlikon engineering works near Zurich took part in this. In the same year Charles Brown and Walter Boveri founded the company BBC in Baden, which later became ABB.

Induction motors are robust, cheap and need hardly any maintenance, because they have no sliding contacts. You find them in washing machines, pumps, ventilation systems, machine tools and ski lifts. Many modern locomotives and trams run on induction motors. A large part of the electricity used in industry is consumed by motors like these.

begriffe.erklaerung: Alternating current from three wires whose voltages are offset in time.
A magnetic field that turns in a circle.
The creation of a current in a conductor by a changing magnetic field.
How much more slowly the rotor turns compared with the rotating field.
A device that changes the frequency of the current and so controls the motor speed.

gewusst: The rotor of a squirrel-cage motor has no electrical connection at all.
Induction motors can also work as generators if you drive them faster than the rotating field.
An induction motor can run for many decades; often only the ball bearings need replacing.

teile.einleitung: An astronaut is a person who flies into space in a spacecraft. Astronauts do research on space stations, repair satellites and have even been to the Moon. For this they need long, hard training.
wichtigste: A person who flies into space is called an astronaut.
Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space in 1961.
Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon in 1969.
Today astronauts often live for months on the International Space Station, ISS.
The ISS takes about an hour and a half to go once round the Earth.
A spacesuit gives astronauts air outside in space and protects them.
Claude Nicollier was the first Swiss astronaut.

abschnitte.text: The word **astronaut** comes from Greek and means star sailor. In Russia people say **cosmonaut**, and in China taikonaut. Astronauts are often pilots, engineers, doctors or scientists. Before they are allowed into space, they train for years, for example under water, in a flight simulator and on language courses.

On 12 April 1961 the Russian **Yuri Gagarin** became the first person to orbit the Earth. In 1963 Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space. In 1969 **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon, on the Apollo 11 mission. Up to 1972 a total of twelve men landed on the Moon. In 1971 Alan Shepard even played golf there.

Since 2000 people have lived permanently on the **International Space Station ISS**. It flies at a height of around 400 kilometres and takes about an hour and a half to orbit the Earth. That is why the astronauts see many sunrises and sunsets every day. Because everything floats, they sleep in sleeping bags tied in place and drink from pouches. They do research, for example, on plants, materials and their own bodies.

In **weightlessness** muscles and bones hardly have to work and quickly become weak. That is why astronauts on the space station do around two hours of exercise every day, for example on a treadmill and an exercise bike with straps. They also get a little taller in space, because the spine stretches. Back on Earth they shrink back to their normal height. Outside in space they wear a **spacesuit**, which gives them air and protects them from cold, heat and radiation.

The astrophysicist **Claude Nicollier** from the canton of Vaud was the first Swiss person in space. Between 1992 and 1999 he flew four times on the American Space Shuttle. Among other things he helped to repair the Hubble Space Telescope. In 2022 the European Space Agency ESA chose the Swiss Marco Sieber for its astronaut team.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state in which you and everything around you float freely.
A large spacecraft that orbits the Earth and in which people live and do research.
A protective suit with an air supply for work outside the spacecraft.
The Russian name for a space traveller.

gewusst: On the ISS, sweat and urine are turned back into drinking water.
The astronauts’ footprints on the Moon are still there today, because there is no wind.
Astronauts cannot cry in space the way they do on Earth, because the tears stick to the eye as a ball.

teile.einleitung: The atomic nucleus is the tiny centre of every atom. It is much smaller than the whole atom, but contains almost all of its mass. Inside it are enormous forces and energies that make stars shine and produce electricity in nuclear power stations.
wichtigste: An atomic nucleus consists of protons and neutrons.
The general term for the particles in the nucleus is nucleons.
Almost all the mass of an atom is in the nucleus.
The strong nuclear force holds the nucleus together, even though the protons repel each other.
The number of protons determines which chemical element it is.
In chemical reactions the atomic nucleus stays unchanged.
Ernest Rutherford discovered the atomic nucleus in 1911.

abschnitte.text: An atom consists of a shell of electrons and a nucleus in the middle. The nucleus is built of **protons** and **neutrons**, which together are called **nucleons**. Protons are positively charged; neutrons have no charge. The number of protons decides which element it is: hydrogen has one proton, carbon six and iron 26. Atoms of an element with different numbers of neutrons are called **isotopes**.

The atomic nucleus is about 10,000 to 100,000 times smaller than the whole atom. If an atom were as big as a football stadium, the nucleus would only be the size of a pea on the centre spot. Even so, almost all the mass is in it. A teaspoon of pure nuclear matter would therefore weigh around a billion tonnes. In neutron stars such unimaginably dense matter really exists.

Protons with the same charge repel each other electrically. The fact that the nucleus does not fly apart anyway is due to the **strong nuclear force**. It is much stronger than the electrical repulsion, but only acts over tiny distances. When protons and neutrons join to form a nucleus, **binding energy** is released. Some nuclei are unstable and break down by themselves; this is called radioactivity.

In 1911 **Ernest Rutherford** and his team fired alpha particles at a very thin gold foil. Most went straight through, but some bounced back. From this Rutherford concluded that an atom has a tiny, heavy nucleus. In 1932 James Chadwick discovered the neutron. In 1938 Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found out that uranium nuclei can be split.

In **nuclear fission** a heavy nucleus such as uranium breaks into lighter pieces, releasing energy. This is how the Swiss nuclear power stations Beznau, Gösgen and Leibstadt work. In **nuclear fusion** light nuclei such as hydrogen fuse into heavier ones. This is how the sun shines. In stars, fusion only releases energy up to the element iron, which is why it stops there.

At EPFL in Lausanne there is the fusion research facility **TCV**, a so-called tokamak. In it extremely hot gas is held in place by magnetic fields in order to study nuclear fusion. At CERN near Geneva researchers study what protons and neutrons themselves are made of. They are in fact built of even smaller particles, the quarks. The Paul Scherrer Institute in Aargau also does research with neutrons.

begriffe.erklaerung: A positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.
An uncharged particle in the atomic nucleus.
The general term for protons and neutrons.
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
The force that holds the particles in the atomic nucleus together.

gewusst: Rutherford said that the particles bouncing back was as incredible as if a shell had bounced off a piece of tissue paper.
Your body consists almost entirely of empty space, because atomic nuclei are so tiny.
All elements heavier than iron were created in huge star explosions and collisions of stars.

teile.einleitung: Buoyancy is a force that pushes objects upwards in liquids and gases. It makes ships float and balloons rise. The force that keeps an aeroplane in the air is also called lift.
wichtigste: Buoyancy is an upward force in liquids and gases.
A body experiences as much buoyancy as the water or gas it displaces weighs.
This rule is called Archimedes’ principle.
If the buoyancy is greater than the weight, a body floats or rises.
Hot-air balloons rise because warm air is lighter than cold air.
The force that keeps an aeroplane in the air is called lift.
Aeroplanes get lift from the shape and angle of their wings.

abschnitte.text: When you get into the bath, you feel lighter. The water presses harder against your body from below than from above, because water pressure increases with depth. This difference produces an upward force, **buoyancy**. It acts in all liquids and gases, and so also in air.

The Greek scholar Archimedes lived in the 3rd century BC in Syracuse. He recognised that a body experiences as much buoyancy as the displaced liquid weighs. This rule is called **Archimedes’ principle**. According to legend he shouted “Eureka!” when he came up with it in the bath.

If an object is heavier than the water it displaces, it sinks. If it is lighter, it floats and partly sticks out. A steel ship floats because its hull is hollow and displaces a lot of water. A **submarine** can fill tanks with water or empty them with air and so dive, hover or surface.

There is buoyancy in air too, but it is much smaller, because air is very light. A **hot-air balloon** rises because the heated air in the envelope is less dense than the cold air outside. Balloons filled with helium rise because helium is much lighter than air. Every January a well-known international balloon festival takes place in Château-d'Oex in the canton of Vaud.

An aeroplane is much heavier than the air it displaces. It therefore needs a different kind of upward force, **dynamic lift**. The curved wings, tilted slightly, deflect the air flowing past them downwards. This creates lower pressure above the wing and higher pressure below it, which pushes the aeroplane upwards. The faster an aeroplane flies, the greater this lift.

begriffe.erklaerung: A force that pushes upwards in water or air.
The amount of water or air that a body pushes aside.
How much mass there is in a certain volume.
The specially shaped wing of an aeroplane that produces lift.

gewusst: In the Dead Sea the water is so salty and dense that people lie on top of it like a cork.
A large cruise ship displaces many tens of thousands of tonnes of water and still floats.
